extracted.intended_audience: librarians, educators, policymakers, and general readers interested in censorship and educational resources
extracted.subtask_description: A topical encyclopedic overview of political, legislative, legal, and operational standards and actions aimed at restricting or regulating content in educational research databases used by K-12, public, and postsecondary libraries in the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: State legislative verification and filtering requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills require companies providing K-12 databases to verify that database content is free of obscene or pornographic content, requiring filtering of said content, and nullifying the contracts with any vendor that is believed to have served up such content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language for these bills is similar across states (Idaho, Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Mississippi, etc.). Example: Idaho HB522 (codified as Section 33-137) and other state bills require vendors to demonstrate compliance or face contract termination. The page notes these bills often mirror already-existing K-12 internet use policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of educational-value exception from obscenity law
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation (e.g., Tennessee) removes protections for materials with educational value from being defined as 'obscene.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing the educational-value exception expands the range of curricular and co-curricular materials that can be blocked or criminalized; Tennessee's change is cited as an example of broadening what can be censored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal or personal liability for librarians and educators
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proposed laws criminalize librarians and educators, making them personally—and often criminally—liable for allowing minors to access resources with content about human sexuality, and possibly race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oklahoma's HB3702 and similar proposals remove exemptions for 'employees of school districts, charter schools, ... public libraries, and universities' who create 'willful violations.' This shifts enforcement from vendors to individual staff and may force changes to library practice (e.g., mediated searches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual student login and parental-access requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation (e.g., Nebraska LB1213/LB635 drafts) may require each student to have an individual username and password, and require that each student's username and password be given to the student's parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical database access is IP-based (single school login); moving to per-student credentials creates large administrative burdens (example: a 3,000-student high school needing 3,000 accounts) and raises privacy/operational concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redefinition of 'sexually explicit' or 'harmful to minors' to avoid established legal tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states propose or pass laws that sidestep established obscenity tests (like Miller) by legislating against 'sexually explicit materials' or broadly defining 'harmful to minors' without settled legal definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using undefined or broader terms makes it easier for policymakers/activists to expand the net of banned or filtered materials beyond what the Miller Test would permit, increasing uncertainty for librarians and vendors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efforts to curtail the Miller Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Where legislating about databases specifically has been unsuccessful, activists have moved to attempting to curtail the long-held legal definition of 'obscenity,' as defined by the United States Supreme Court in Miller v. California (the Miller Test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites Tennessee's legislative changes as an example of removing protections and altering the practical operation of the Miller Test for educational materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor mitigation: audits, functionality tweaks, and local controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Database providers have responded by auditing content/behavior, tweaking functionality, creating local controls so districts/states can block certain resources, and proactively censoring search terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: EBSCO audited selection processes and clarified policies; EBSCO created local controls for districts/states after Utah's temporary shutdown; some companies (e.g., Gale K-12) make certain terms unsearchable nationwide (e.g., forms of the word 'sex'). These are vendor-level compliance or damage-control measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: School/institutional filtering tied to federal funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools already filter web-based content, including educational research databases, in order to receive federal funding for internet access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This references existing obligations (e.g., related to federal program rules like CIPA/E-Rate) that require filtering as a practical baseline constraint for school-provided internet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and replicability standard for claims of objectionable content
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that educational research databases include pornographic or obscene materials often rely on 'database hopping' (following links out to the open web) and have not been replicable when tested by experts or vendors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that many reported problematic search results could not be reproduced by researchers, database companies (EBSCO), or oversight bodies, which weakens activists' evidentiary claims (examples: Cherry Creek, Utah investigations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and reporting as a compliance/oversight practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Some network operators and states monitor database use, block search terms, and publish quarterly reports (including word clouds) to demonstrate appropriate or inappropriate usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Utah Education Network blocks over 15,000 search terms and issues quarterly monitoring reports; such monitoring is used to argue that students do not run inappropriate searches and to justify reinstating access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract cancellation and the 'chilling effect' on access
rubrics_metrics.description: Political pressure and censorship challenges have prompted school districts to cancel vendor contracts and remove access to databases, creating a chilling effect on students' access to information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Over 130 school districts canceled EBSCO contracts; loss of access removed tens of thousands of titles and millions of articles (estimate given: almost 97,000 titles / more than 175 million articles). The article frames proactive dropping of resources as stemming from fear of activism or misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation of restrictions between K-12 and postsecondary users
rubrics_metrics.description: Some legislation carves out post-secondary students or dual-enrollment participants from K-12 restrictions, exempting them from the stricter limits applied to K-12 access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mississippi HB1315 specified that post-secondary students, including dual-enrollment students, were not held to the same restrictions as most K-12 students; Oklahoma later passed SB2247 to spell out that post-secondary institutions were not subject to HB3702.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration and local-review policies for disputed content
rubrics_metrics.description: Some schools and districts follow established reconsideration policies and local reviews, concluding that databases do not contain obscene content under legal definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that districts following reconsideration procedures sometimes find the content is legally permissible; this is presented as an alternative to immediate removal or legislative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational/educational impacts of access restrictions (research capability loss)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blocking or removing access to databases can hamper advanced research and learning, e.g., high school students losing independent access to advanced sources required for coursework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Oklahoma law resulted in high-achieving students being unable to undertake required research; the University of Oklahoma instituted mediated searches, undermining students' development of research skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims-sourcing problems: evidence often originates from non-student searches
rubrics_metrics.description: In documented cases of 'pornographic' or 'obscene' discoveries, the individuals finding the content frequently were not students but adults following paths from databases to the open web.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cherry Creek and other cases are cited where parents or activists—not children—accessed open-web sites via links in database content (e.g., embedded links in mainstream magazine articles), illustrating a common anti-pattern in complaints.
